title: Spacetime Quasicrystals and Computational Complexity Theory in the Road Towards Quantum Gravity
abstract: Part I: Semiclassical Gravity Efficiently Solves $\mathsf{NP}$-Complete Problems   Assuming the gravitational field is classical and that it couples to quantum fields via the semiclassical Einstein field equations (EFEs), we show that the weak-field dynamics of a massive and non-relativistic qubit can in principle be used to solve an $\mathsf{NP}$-complete problem in polynomial time. We attribute this vast computational power to the non-linear qubit dynamics afforded by the semiclassical EFEs. Consequently, the above two assumptions entail a violation of the Physical Extended Church--Turing Thesis, which we regard as evidence for the quantization of gravity.   Part II: Spacetime Quasicrystals   We generalize self-similar quasicrystals, such as the Penrose tilings, from Euclidean space to Minkowski spacetime. We construct the first examples of Lorentzian quasicrystals and identify their key novel features. We then explore possible connections to fundamental physics. First, we propose a speculative scenario in which our $(3+1)$D universe is embedded in a particularly symmetric $(9+1)$D torus $\mathbb{T}^{9,1}$, previously identified as the most symmetric toroidal compactification of the superstring. We suggest that this construction may shed light on the seesaw relation $M_{\rm Pl}M_{\rm vac} \approx M_{\rm EW}^{2}$ between the Planck, vacuum-energy, and electroweak scales. Second, we replace the random causal sets of causal set theory with ordered, highly symmetric quasi-crystalline causal sets. We find suggestive evidence that our quasicrystals outperform Poisson random sets in the number-volume correspondence in both $(1+1)$D and $(3+1)$D, where such behaviour has been conjectured to be impossible. Finally, extending hyperuniformity from space to spacetime, we show that our $(1+1)$D quasicrystal is the first demonstrated example of a spacetime-hyperuniform structure.
summary: This paper bridges quantum gravity, computational complexity, and geometry by examining spacetime quasicrystals. It argues that semiclassical gravity implies computational power beyond classical limits, suggesting quantum gravity. Furthermore, it develops the theory of Lorentzian quasicrystals and uses N-V tests to confirm their unique, hyperuniform structure in spacetime.
main_problem: The paper explores the deep connections between solving computationally hard problems, the structure of spacetime geometry via quasicrystals, and the fundamental principles of quantum gravity.
main_result: The authors show that semiclassical gravity dynamics can violate the Physical Extended Church–Turing Thesis, suggesting quantum gravity, and they establish that spacetime quasicrystals exhibit novel properties like spacetime hyperuniformity.
method: The work employs two main theoretical approaches: analyzing the weak-field dynamics of qubits coupled to classical gravity, and performing Number-Volume (N-V) tests on constructed Lorentzian quasicrystals in Minkowski spacetime.
model_or_system: The models include the dynamics of a massive qubit under semiclassical Einstein field equations, and the construction/analysis of Lorentzian quasicrystals, which are generalizations of Penrose tilings to spacetime.
key_observables: Computational complexity (NP-completeness), violation of the Physical Extended Church–Turing Thesis, Number-Volume counts ($\langle Nangle$), and the standard deviation of point counts ($\sigma_{N\diamond}$).
important_parameters: The Planck scale ($M_{m Pl}$), vacuum energy scale ($M_{m vac}$), electroweak scale ($M_{m EW}$), and the dimensionality of spacetime (e.g., (3+1)D).
main_assumptions: The analysis in Part I assumes the gravitational field is classical and couples semiclassically to quantum fields. Part II relies on constructing highly symmetric quasi-crystalline causal sets.
figures_summary: The figures present extensive N-V test data for various lattices (Poisson, integer, Fibonacci) in (2+1)D and (3+1)D, illustrating how the standard deviation of point counts ($\sigma_{N\diamond}$) varies with the boost parameter, demonstrating structural differences.
paper_structure: The paper is divided into two parts: Part I addresses the computational power derived from semiclassical gravity, leading to a violation of the Church–Turing Thesis. Part II generalizes quasicrystals to Minkowski spacetime, proposing connections to string theory compactifications and testing their hyperuniformity via N-V tests.
why_interesting: While not directly focused on AMO systems, the study of non-linear dynamics (qubits in curved spacetime) and the use of advanced mathematical structures (quasicrystals) to model fundamental physics are highly relevant to theoretical quantum information and quantum gravity research.

figures.caption: Figure 1.1: Left: a patch of the Penrose tiling [54] given by rhombs in purple, underlaid by its “inflation” in pink. Right top: the thin (red) and thick (blue) Penrose rhombs, along with their edge-matching rules and inflation rules. Right bottom: Conway’s version of the tiles: “darts” (red) and “kites” (blue) are given with their inflation rules. The two versions are equivalent since tilings built from kites and darts are mutually locally derivable from tilings by rhombs. For an introduction to the Penrose tiling, see Ref. [55]. Figure created by Latham Boyle and reproduced from [68].

Figure 2.1: Some relevant complexity classes and their interrelations (see text for formal definitions). P contains problems that can be solved “quickly” (i.e. in polynomial time), while problems in NP can have their solutions verified “quickly” (see Fig. 2.2). Both P and NP contain decision problems. NP-hard contains problems that need not be themselves decision problems nor verifiable “quickly”. For example, they might be decision problems that are ‘undecidable’, like the Halting Problem [82, 83]; thus NP-hard is a strict superset of NP. Yet, any NP problem can be mapped to an NP-hard problem “quickly”. In that sense, NP-hard is at least as hard as NP: if a solution to an NP-hard problem...

Figure 2.2: P vs NP: an illustration. A decision problem L is in P if its solution can be found (i.e. it can be decided) by a deterministic Turing machine M in polynomial time (polynomially many “ticks”). A decision problem L is in NP if, provided a witness W supplies us with a proof y that our problem has a solution, M can verify the solution in polynomially many ticks. The proof y must be “written in polynomially many pages” in terms of the size |x| of the input-problem.

Figure 4.1: An example of a non-isometric diffeomorphism of the sphere S2: a position- dependent rotation. This twists the sphere and stretches the distance between two grey points that were originally along the same meridian. Due to the differential rotation of S2, the grey point on the z = 0 slice rotates faster than that on the z = z0 slice, leading to the blue points after the map τS2 is applied which are now further apart. On the other hand, the isometric diffeomorphism πS2 rotates all points at the same rate and preserves the original grey distance between the points.

Figure 6.1: The Coxeter-Dynkin diagrams for the irreducible Coxeter groups of fi- nite/spherical type (left panel) and affine/planar type (right panel). The non- crystallographic cases (H4, H3 and In 2 ) are grouped in the box in the lower left. Each affine diagram (at right) may be obtained by adding a single “extending root” to the cor- responding finite crystallographic diagram (at left); or, alternatively, by removing a single extending node (any of the black nodes) from any affine diagram (at right) we obtain the corresponding finite crystallographic diagram (at left).
